# Corridor Planning Proposal: New York City to Chicago Intercity Passenger Rail

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal provides an early planning evaluation of three conceptual passenger rail alternatives connecting New York City, NY, and Chicago, IL. Modeled options include two paths utilizing existing rights-of-way—the Lake Shore corridor upgrade and the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade—alongside the New direct high-speed alignment, which follows a greenfield route across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Across 5000 simulation runs per alternative, outcomes vary significantly across alignment length, track construction requirements, community proximity, cost benchmarks, and delivery timelines.

Capital figures evaluated in this screening are illustrative estimates rather than engineered budgets, derived from broad per-mile benchmarks rather than detailed site design. Proximity metrics indicate substantial populations residing within 10 miles of each alignment, though population counts do not represent passenger ridership forecasts. Similarly, utilizing existing rail rights-of-way does not confirm corridor access, operating permissions, or spare capacity from host freight carriers. This proposal outlines the comparative trade-offs between legacy corridor enhancements and greenfield development under explicit planning assumptions.

## Service Assumptions

No train service plan has been defined for this corridor. Key operating parameters—including service frequency, timetables, stopping patterns, train speeds, and fares—remain entirely open. Stations are conceptually assumed at cities within 5 km of an alignment; specific station sites and facilities have not been selected.

Travel times have not been estimated, meaning alignment length cannot be interpreted as a measure of trip time. Furthermore, operations on existing rail corridors would require sharing track with freight traffic under operating agreements that do not currently exist.

## Alternatives and Tradeoffs

Alternative 1, the Lake Shore corridor upgrade, spans 954 miles upgrading the water-level route via Albany, Buffalo, Cleveland, and Toledo along the path of Amtrak's Lake Shore Limited. It features a 99.7% share on existing rail corridors, 3 miles of new track, 0 miles of new track in flagged areas, 20 environmental flag entries, and 20 river crossings. It links 11 stations (New York City, Poughkeepsie, Albany, Utica, Syracuse, Buffalo, Erie, Cleveland, Toledo, South Bend, and Chicago), with 22.23 million residents within 10 miles of the line and 7.41 million residents within 10 km of stations.

Alternative 2, the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade, spans 858 miles across the Appalachians via Philadelphia, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, and Fort Wayne, utilizing the Northeast Corridor, Keystone Corridor, and former Pennsylvania Railroad main lines. It incorporates a 99.9% share on existing rail corridors, 1 miles of new track, 0 miles of new track in flagged areas, 10 environmental flag entries, and 11 river crossings. Serving 6 stations (New York City, Philadelphia, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Chicago), it counts 22.33 million residents near the alignment and 7.54 million residents near stations.

Alternative 3, the New direct high-speed alignment, spans 743 miles on a greenfield path across Pennsylvania and Ohio designed to minimize distance. It has a 23.1% share on existing rail corridors, 571 miles of new track, 5 miles of new track in flagged areas, 7 environmental flag entries, and 5 river crossings. It features 2 stations (New York City and Chicago), with 16.14 million residents along the line and 5.31 million residents near stations.

## Recommendation Under the Stated Priorities

Under the stated scenario priorities—Lower capital cost (35%), More residents near stations (25%), Faster delivery (20%), and Less new track in flagged areas (20%)—the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade leads the comparative ranking, followed by the Lake Shore corridor upgrade and the New direct high-speed alignment. The top two options are not considered a close call under this weighting framework.

This ranking is strictly conditional on the assigned weights and reflects a mathematical comparison of the modeled measures only. It does not establish that the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade is the best project, nor does it demonstrate financial feasibility, grant eligibility, potential ridership, or value for money.

## Cost, Schedule and Uncertainty

Modeled costs are illustrative estimates based on placeholder benchmarks bracketed by publicly reported projects, rather than formal budgets. Modeled delivery schedules and costs are derived from 5000 Monte Carlo simulation runs per alternative. The range between P10 and P90 represents the middle 80% of modeled outcomes under the model's own assumptions and does not constitute a guarantee of project parameters.

For the Lake Shore corridor upgrade, capital cost is estimated at $20.3B for P10, $25.2B for median (P50), and $31.4B for P90, with time to opening modeled at 15.4 years (P10), 17.8 years median (P50), and 20.3 years (P90). The Pennsylvania corridor upgrade reflects capital costs of $19.7B for P10, $24.3B for median (P50), and $30.2B for P90, with time to opening estimated at 13.8 years (P10), 15.8 years median (P50), and 17.9 years (P90). The New direct high-speed alignment requires greater investment due to its 571 miles of new track and mountain structures, yielding capital costs of $29.6B for P10, $35.5B for median (P50), and $42.2B for P90, alongside time to opening ranges of 15.9 years (P10), 18.0 years median (P50), and 20.2 years (P90).

## Funding Considerations

Federal funding programs differ substantially in screening fit, statutory grant caps, assumed allocations, and loan mechanisms; no funding is currently secured. Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National) serves as the core capital grant match with a fit score of 0.90 across all alternatives, offering an assumed federal amount of $3.0B (11.9% of median cost for Alternative 1, 12.3% for Alternative 2, and 8.5% for Alternative 3). The program allows up to an 80% federal share, though median project costs exceed the assumed single-award ceiling of $3.0B, requiring capital phasing. The FY2024–2026 round is closed with selections announced August 14, 2026, and no open round is currently listed. The Northeast Corridor component of the program provides a fit score of 0.60 and an assumed $2.1B (8.5% of median cost) for the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade due to its 91 miles on the NEC main line, whereas the Lake Shore corridor upgrade has a lower fit score of 0.35 and an assumed $1.0B (4.0% of median cost) for NEC-adjacent segments; its FY2025–2026 round is closed.

Planning entry is identified through the Corridor Identification and Development Program (fit score 0.95), which provides an initial $500K for Step 1 scoping but currently has no open solicitation since the FY2022 awards. Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements grants present a fit score of 0.80 for Alternatives 1 and 2 and 0.55 for Alternative 3, with an assumed amount of $250M suited for discrete grade separations or sidings; the FY2025–2026 round closed with awards announced October 19, 2026. BUILD grants reflect a fit score of 0.45, capped at $25M per award (representing 0.1% of median cost), suitable only for isolated station or crossing elements, with its FY2026 round closed. Finally, Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing represents a loan program, not a grant, evaluated with an assumed loan amount of $3.0B (fit scores of 0.70 for Alternatives 1 and 2, 0.60 for Alternative 3); this financing requires a dedicated non-federal repayment source. Because the alignments span multiple states—5 states for Alternative 1, 4 states for Alternative 2, and 2 states for Alternative 3—interstate compacts or multi-state sponsors would be necessary.

## Risks and Information Gaps

Project risks are centered on unmodeled operational factors, right-of-way constraints, and financial capacity:

* Unmodeled operational performance: Ridership and station-pair demand forecasts were not modeled, meaning passenger demand is unknown. Similarly, door-to-door or in-train travel times, competitiveness against highway or air modes, on-time performance, and reliability were not analyzed.
* Infrastructure and fleet gaps: Track capacity, train paths, freight conflicts, and access agreements with host railroads are unmodeled; high shares on existing rail corridors (99.7% in Alternative 1 and 99.9% in Alternative 2) do not guarantee capacity or operating rights. Fleet procurement, maintenance facilities, and electrification costs are excluded.
* Financial and life-cycle liabilities: Operating and maintenance costs, fare revenues, annual operating subsidies, and overall benefit-cost ratios were not modeled. Capital estimates are illustrative rather than engineering-grade, and matching requirements exceed single-award program limits.
* Environmental and constructability hurdles: Alternative 1 involves 20 river crossings and 20 environmental flag entries, while Alternative 3 requires 571 miles of new track, including 5 miles in flagged areas, creating extensive right-of-way acquisition and structural delivery risks.

## Next Steps

To address unmodeled gaps and advance corridor planning, the following sequential steps are outlined:

* Establish governance: Form a multi-state working group or interstate compact across participating states (covering up to 5 states depending on the alternative) to establish a unified sponsoring entity.
* Pursue Corridor ID entry: Coordinate with regional partners to identify overlapping corridors or prepare a joint application for the next Corridor ID solicitation to secure Step 1 scoping resources ($500K) and initiate a formal service development plan.
* Conduct ridership and operations modeling: Develop service alternatives evaluating frequencies, stopping patterns, timetables, travel-time competitiveness, fleet requirements, and demand forecasting.
* Initiate host railroad discussions: Begin preliminary technical discussions with host freight railroads to evaluate corridor capacity, track sharing, sidings, and grade crossings.
* Prepare discrete capital packages: Identify standalone safety, station, or grade-crossing packages eligible for future CRISI or BUILD application cycles, and coordinate with the NEC Commission for eligible New York approach elements.
* Define finance and repayment mechanisms: Assess state funding sources, farebox recovery, or value capture mechanisms required to satisfy non-federal grant match obligations and support potential RRIF loan consultations with the Build America Bureau.

## Scenario Record

- Corridor: New York City, NY to Chicago, IL
- Priorities (share of weight): Lower capital cost 35%, Faster delivery 20%, More residents near stations 25%, Less new track in flagged areas 20%
- Ranking under these priorities: Pennsylvania corridor upgrade, Lake Shore corridor upgrade, New direct high-speed alignment
- Selected alternative: Lake Shore corridor upgrade
- Plan 69, model version 2026.10.25-3, 5,000 simulations per alternative
- Draft generated: 2026-10-25 03:51 UTC
